title: Singing ii–V–I with a Lydian finish

review.reviewedBy: Claude, the AI that wrote it

inspiration.note: Metheny's playing has a fluid, singing quality, with a legato approach full of slides and pull-offs, and in 'Phase Dance' he brings out the bright Lydian sound of the raised 4th over the major-seventh chords. This line borrows the singing legato, a slide into the next chord and the Lydian finish.

analysis.summary: A singing line built on wide intervals: two rising 6ths over {{chord 1}}, a slide down a half step into the 3rd of {{chord 2}}, a falling 4th and a rising 5th over {{chord 2}}, and a stepwise fall into the 3rd of {{chord 3}}. From there the line leaps up a 5th and down a 4th to end on the #11, the bright Lydian note.

points.text: Guide tones carry the line: the 7th of {{chord 1}} ({{note 1.5}}), held for two beats, slides down a half step to the 3rd of {{chord 2}} ({{note 2.1}}). Over {{chord 3}} the line states the 3rd and 7th ({{note 3.1}}, {{note 3.2}}) before the colour note.

The 9ths of {{chord 1}} and {{chord 2}} ({{note 1.4}}, {{note 2.4}}) soften the line. The last note, {{note 3.3}}, is the #11 of {{chord 3}}: a raised 4th that gives a major chord the bright, floating Lydian sound. It is also the 5th of the tune's home minor key, a half step below {{key}}, and the home key is exactly where the tune goes next.

{{note 2.6}} is the 7th of {{chord 2}}, and it steps down a half step into the 3rd of {{chord 3}}. That small guide-tone move is what makes the cadence land, so the line can leap freely everywhere else.

The phrase starts on the 'and' of 1 and mixes flowing eighth notes with long notes. The peak of bar 1 is held for two beats, the slide arrives exactly on the chord change, the 3rd of {{chord 3}} lands on beat 1, and the #11 starts on beat 3 and rings to the end.
{{note 3.1}} is the 3rd of {{chord 3}}, arriving on beat 1. Landing on the 3rd first makes the new chord clear, so the #11 that follows sounds like a colour rather than a wrong note.

whyItWorks: Wide leaps sound lyrical when the important moves are small. Here the big intervals are framed by half-step guide-tone moves at both chord changes, so the harmony stays clear. Arriving on the 3rd and then reaching the #11 lets the ear hear the plain major chord first and the Lydian colour second.
fingeringNote: Eighth position in the lesson's original key, one finger per fret. In bar 1 the jump to the long top note skips the B string, and the index finger reaches up one fret for it, then slides back down one fret into bar 2, which brings the hand back to its position. In bar 2, pull off from the pinky to the middle finger on the B string for the note on beat 4. The last two notes sit on the same fret on neighbouring strings: roll the index finger from the high E string to the B string.
practiceTask: Play the lick over bars 9 to 11 of the weekly standard and let the last note ring through bar 12. Keep that note in your ear as the tune returns to its home key in bar 13: it is the 5th of that key.

variation.description: Skip the 3rd and land straight on the colour note: the root of {{chord 2}} falls a half step onto the #11 of {{chord 3}} ({{note 3.1}}) on beat 1, and it rings for three beats. Landing on the #11 is a bolder, more modern sound; compare it with the lick, where the 3rd lands first and the #11 comes last.
